claim: Chunking compiles the result of a subgoal into one rule whose conditions are only the pre-goal data actually accessed. This gives large same-task speed-up (R1-Soar minimal search control: 1731 decisions without learning, 485 with learning in the same run, 7 on rerun; Dispatcher-Soar: a repeated problem takes 4 decision cycles) and some transfer. Both sources come from the Soar group, so independence is weak.
agent_test: Arm A: after each solved sub-problem store a compact note (accessed facts -> result) keyed by those facts. Arm B: no store. Same token budget. Measure tokens to solve a repeated item and a near-variant item.

claim: Chunking learning curves look like a power law in decision cycles (Dispatcher-Soar, 10 probe problems, roughly straight on log-log axes, overall speed-up factor 7), but this is a visual fit and no exponential form was fitted. On the human-data side, averaged curves bias toward a power law; individual curves favour exponential (Heathcote 2000, Evans 2018) while Rickard 1997 finds power laws inside each strategy. Human-data papers were read as abstracts or snippets only. Gap search (d15, d16, d08): the human abstracts say per-participant exponential fits beat power fits (40 data sets, 7,910 series) and a delayed exponential wins in most paradigms (Evans 2018); full texts still unread. For an LLM store, the only per-run numbers found (APC cold start, 5 points) fit a straight line best, exponential next, power law worst. This does not settle the Soar curves.
agent_test: Fit power, exponential and delayed-exponential to our agent's tokens-per-item over item index, per run and not averaged. Report which form wins.

claim: Only a small share of learned rules ever transfers. In Dispatcher-Soar 10.3% of 10,112 chunks transferred to a later problem, 42 of 200 problems needed no database look-up, transfer share ranged from 0% to 100% by problem space, and 55 chunks in one space never transferred because parent-space chunks fired first. Most gain comes from a few often-reused chunks.
agent_test: Log reuse count per stored procedure over a 200-item stream. Check what share of the gain comes from the top 10% of entries. Test pruning never-reused entries at equal tokens.

claim: A single learned rule can cost so much to match that it erases the savings. Kim and Rosenbloom: linear rule learning took 1.42 s per problem vs 0.46 s without learning (3.1x slower) and nonlinear learning 0.34 s; one Magic Square rule reached over 8 million partial matches and ran out of memory. Tambe et al. (abstract only) show the same and propose restricting rule form. Minton's utility problem is the same idea in EBL.
agent_test: Measure tokens spent applying a stored procedure vs tokens it saves. Flag entries with net negative value (long skills, many preconditions to check) and drop them.

claim: On average, match cost did not grow over 10,112 chunks (token changes per decision cycle flat or slightly falling), against the utility-problem prediction. But wall-clock time per decision cycle still rose 0.47 s per 10,000 chunks and the Rete network grew eight-fold. The utility problem is real for individual rules; for the average rule in this one system it did not show up.
agent_test: Grow the library 10, 100, 1000 entries. Plot tokens in context and success. Look for the knee.

claim: Chunks can be over-general: they fire where the original reasoning would not. Documented causes: special-case knowledge that was almost satisfied is not recorded (Tic-Tac-Toe chunk tests A,B,C,E,I,G,F but not D or H), local negations, recalled memory treated as local, tests on impasse existence, random or probabilistic operator choice, untracked search-control preferences. Soar keeps learning off by default and now filters or refuses these cases. ACT-R authors blame over-generalisation on reusing old experience.
agent_test: Seed the store with procedures that miss one precondition. Measure how often the agent applies them wrongly with and without an explicit precondition-check step.

claim: ACT-R production compilation (merge two rules that fire in sequence, folding the retrieval in) fits human practice curves: r2 .97 for planes landed, .98 land unit task, .91 and .87 for two other levels (65 students, 18 trials, default parameters) and it gives U-shaped past-tense learning. All from one research group; the model is slower or faster than people on some unit tasks.
agent_test: No direct test. Use as a design rule: compile a pattern only after it has fired several times (experience threshold).

claim: Workflow memory (reusable routines induced from the agent's own successful runs) improves a web agent: WebArena GPT-4 23.5 -> 35.5 (+12.0 points, +51.1% relative), about 2 fewer steps. The gain shrinks with a stronger base: Claude-3.5 vanilla 32.7 -> AWM 36.3 (+3.6); ReasoningBank reports AWM 40.8 vs 41.7 no-memory for Claude-3.7 (a loss). Baselines also differ by paper (GPT-4 vanilla 23.5 in AWM, 12.3 in ASI). Gap search: the gain is gated by two things, not only by base strength. Small models fail to write or use entries (Dynamic Cheatsheet: Haiku and GPT-4o-mini near zero or negative), and gains are small on strong models in streams without repeated structure (Evo-Memory, Claude 3.7 Sonnet single-turn: baseline 0.54, most modules 0.48 to 0.59). ACE on GPT-5.1 (base 54.2) still gained about +6 to +11.6. Still no measurement on our base model.
agent_test: Run our agent with and without a workflow store on the same tasks at equal tokens, with a strong and a weak base model. Expect a larger gain for the weak one.

claim: Workflow gains are large on step success but small on whole-task success on hard tasks. Mind2Web cross-task step success 36.2 -> 45.1, task success 2.0 -> 4.8; cross-domain step 18.6 -> 32.6 offline and 35.5 online, task 1.0 -> 0.7 offline and 1.7 online; cross-task action F1 fell 60.6 -> 57.3. Gains fall as the train-test gap widens; online induction holds up better.
agent_test: Report step-level and item-level success separately for any memory arm. A step gain that does not move item accuracy is not a win.

claim: Execution-checking a candidate skill before storing it helps. ASI Shopping: unverified text 32.6, verified text 39.0, verified program in memory 36.4, verified program as callable action 40.1; only 15.6% of program inductions passed vs 31.4% of AWM adds. Voyager: removing self-verification cut discovered items 73%. Xiong: strict evaluator on add gave 38.50 on EHRAgent vs 16.75 fixed and 13.05 add-all.
agent_test: Gate the store write on a re-run check of the procedure on its source item. Compare gated vs ungated stores at equal tokens, counting the check tokens.

claim: Adding every experience to memory makes agents worse than a small fixed memory: add-all below fixed on all four agents (RegAgent 55.48 vs 67.53; EHRAgent 13.05 vs 16.75; AgentDriver 32.32 vs 40.11; CIC-IoT 59.90 vs 71.50), because agents copy the outputs of similar stored items. A retrieval pool of 34,198 real skills moves benefit toward the no-skill level, and 4+ skills per task gave +5.9 vs +18.6 for 2-3. Gap search: full-history append gave 26.7 vs baseline 23.3 for Sonnet but 6.7 vs 20.0 for GPT-4o on AIME 2024 (Dynamic Cheatsheet); a full rewrite of the store collapsed 18,282 tokens to 122 and accuracy 66.7 to 57.1 (ACE); retrieving too many entries lowers accuracy after a plateau (Memp).
agent_test: Compare add-all, strict-add and fixed-size stores. Also inject one wrong entry into a store of similar items and measure how often the error is copied.

claim: Skills written by the model itself give about no average gain while curated skills do (SkillsBench: 24.3 -> 40.6, +16.2 points; self-generated mean 21.0 over the 5 configs that were run, delta -1.3 in one table and -1.8 in another; 16 of 84 tasks worse with skills). But execution-grounded self-induction helped on web tasks (ASI +7.7 over vanilla, SkillWeaver +32%). The split is unverified self-written text (fails) vs verified or executed procedures (can win).
agent_test: Three arms at equal tokens including authoring cost: no skills, self-written unverified, self-written verified by execution.

claim: Chunk grain size matters. Skills induced from whole tasks tend to hurt, skills induced per sub-task help (11-model average over AppWorld, OfficeBench, KramaBench: task-level none 22.1, text 20.9, code 18.0; sub-task none 24.8, text 26.7, code 25.3; GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld 27.3 -> 1.0 with task-level code skills). The task-level text drop lies inside the confidence intervals; only the code drop is clear.
agent_test: From the same trajectories, store whole-solution procedures vs per-subgoal procedures and compare.

claim: State 'in SkillsBench v1' or use v4 numbers (comprehensive documentation roughly flat, +0.7 to -2.9; 4+ skills lose most of the gain); describe the Soar link as an analogy about expensive learned-rule matching, not 'big rules'.
agent_test: Cap stored procedure length at three tiers and compare success at equal tokens.
audit_note: The +17.8/+18.6/+5.9 and +18.8/+17.1/+10.1/-2.9 figures match SkillsBench v1 only; the current v4 reports 1 skill +18.0, 2-3 +19.0, 4+ +10.1 and compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7, and Kim & Rosenbloom (Grid 0.46/1.42/0.34 s verified) is about match structure, not rule size.
claim_before_audit: Compact or detailed single skills beat comprehensive documentation (SkillsBench: detailed +18.8, compact +17.1, standard +10.1, comprehensive -2.9; 1 skill +17.8, 2-3 skills +18.6, 4+ skills +5.9). This agrees with the Soar finding that big learned rules cost more than they save (K04).

claim: Voyager's skill library pays late and in transfer; other parts matter more. Without the library, early milestones are as fast (wooden 7 vs 6, stone 9 vs 11, iron 29 vs 21 iterations) but the diamond tool is not reached. In a fresh world with the library all 4 tasks were solved 3/3 (diamond pickaxe 19 vs 36 and 2/3 without). Random curriculum cut items 93%; no self-verification cut them 73%. Only 3 trials per cell, one game.
agent_test: Replicate the shape on a text domain: library on/off x curriculum ordered/random x verification on/off.

claim: A learned library can be handed to another agent. AutoGPT with Voyager's library solved diamond pickaxe 1/3, golden sword 1/3, compass 2/3, lava bucket 0/3 vs 0/3 alone. SkillWeaver skills from a strong model lifted weaker ones. Haiku 4.5 with skills (27.7) beat Opus 4.5 without (22.0) on SkillsBench. Gains are partial and fragile (cross-website ASI vs AWM success p=0.167). Gap search: LATM tools written by GPT-4 let GPT-3.5 reach GPT-4 level on 5 of 6 tasks; Memp memory from GPT-4o gave Qwen2.5-14B +5 percent success and 1.6 fewer steps on TravelPlanner. The maker must be strong (see K29).
agent_test: Build the store with a strong-model run, give it to a weak-model run, compare to the weak model alone at equal tokens.

claim: Failure trajectories help only if the memory is written to use them. With failures added, ReasoningBank rose 46.5 -> 49.7 and Synapse 40.6 -> 41.7 but AWM fell 44.4 -> 42.2 (WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash). ExpeL insight extraction: HotpotQA 28.0 -> 39.0, ALFWorld 40.0 -> 59.0; insights matter more on reasoning, raw trajectories more on ALFWorld (retrieve-only 55 vs insights-only 50). Gap search: in Evo-Memory with failed experiences stored, generic modules (DC-Cu, DC-RS, AWM) drop while the refining ReMem holds; cells uncertain in the text extraction.
agent_test: For failed items store a lesson ('this approach failed because X') vs the raw trace and compare.

claim: Offline and online workflow induction do not add up: Mind2Web cross-task task success offline 4.8, online 4.0, both 1.6. Induced workflows were used often (utility rate 0.94 WebArena, 0.91 Mind2Web) but covered only 0.40 of Mind2Web test steps.
agent_test: Check whether an old store lowers the quality of newly induced entries (dedupe and merge test).

claim: LM-induced abstract workflows beat copied action sequences on Mind2Web (cross-task step success 45.1 vs 43.4, task success 4.8 vs 2.0) and tie on WebArena (35.5 vs 35.6, 5.9 vs 6.3 steps). This is the LLM version of Soar implicit generalisation (keep only accessed data) but the margin is small and from one benchmark pair.
agent_test: Store a procedure with literal values vs with slots. Test on a variant item set.

claim: A hybrid where Soar asks an LLM only on a tie impasse and chunks the answer cuts LLM calls (CogRec: about 500 bootstrap rules; without chunking performance approaches LLM-Direct; call frequency falls to a low plateau; figures only). NL2GenSym: execution feedback from Soar is the key part; removing the critic cut success 23% overall and 37% on hard cases. Gap search: Agentic Plan Caching shows the same effect without Soar on non-recommendation workloads (FinanceBench, QASPER, TabMWP-like math, AIME, GAIA): cost -50.31% and latency -27.28% at 96.61% of full-model accuracy, FinanceBench $4.03 at 91.0% to $1.86 at 85.5%. Gap 10 is partly closed for plan templates; a Soar-style compiled impasse rule is still untested.
agent_test: On repeated impasse types, cache the resolved decision as a rule. Measure LLM calls per item over a stream at equal accuracy.

claim: A 2026 review says no current LLM system compiles the dependency structure of a scoped impasse resolution into a reusable rule; Reflexion and AgentHER match Soar chunking only functionally (evidence level E3). This is a position, not a measurement.
agent_test: Compare a cache keyed by accessed facts (chunk-style) with one keyed by free-text task description on a variant stream.

claim: Two LLM systems already write to the store only on a miss or on novelty: Agentic Plan Caching stores a plan template only after a cache miss followed by a successful run (entity names stripped, keyed by an intent keyword); Buffer of Thoughts stores a template only when its maximum similarity to stored templates is below a threshold. Neither compares this with write-after-every-success, and neither keys by the facts accessed (Memp's fact-averaged key beat a query key by about 2.6 points on GPT-4o commonsense, a small effect). The impasse-triggered write that Soar uses is therefore plausible and used, but its benefit over write-always is unmeasured.
agent_test: Three arms at equal token budget: no store with the same instructions, write after every verified success, write only after an impasse resolved and verified. Key by accessed facts. Report accuracy, hit rate and tokens per item over the same stream.

claim: Part of any measured memory gain is a prompt or format effect, not the stored content. Dynamic Cheatsheet's empty-memory control with the same instructions gave 36.7 vs 23.3 baseline and 50.0 with memory on Sonnet AIME 2024 (about half the gain without any content). Memp's random retrieval gave about 65 percent of the commonsense gain of the best key on GPT-4o (74.59 vs 76.02, from 71.93). A memory result without a same-instruction empty arm cannot be credited to the store.
agent_test: Always include a no-memory arm with the same length and instruction text, and a random-entry arm, before reading any gain as content.

claim: Authoring cost is small next to serving cost when authoring is cheap, and large when a strong model must discover the procedure. Measured: cache generation and keyword extraction were 1.15 percent of cost on FinanceBench and 1.33 percent with zero hits, so break-even is near a 1 percent hit rate (derived); building a rule manual on ALFWorld cost about $14 for 36 tasks; LATM's cost is O(nc + C) with C more than 15 times c; ACE cut adaptation cost 75 to 84 percent against GEPA and Dynamic Cheatsheet. No source reports tokens per stored item at 20, 50 and 200 items for reasoning tasks.
agent_test: Log authoring tokens (writer plus checker) per entry and serving tokens saved per hit; report cumulative net tokens at 20, 50, 200 items.

claim: Wrong application of a stored entry happens and is measurable. With semantic or full-history caches, accuracy on hits is clearly lower than on misses; loosening a keyword match from exact to 0.8 and 0.6 raised hit rate from 46 to 54 and 64 percent and cut accuracy from 85.5 to 83.0 and 77.0. A dispatcher that decides reuse versus new is wrong about 4 to 5 percent of the time (LATM). Replaying a retrieved workflow as is scored 58.18 vs 61.21 when adapted and 55.15 with no memory (Agent KB). AutoManual reports path dependence from raw saved skills. No study applies an explicit precondition check and measures the wrong-application rate before and after.
agent_test: Log every reuse, and score each as applicable or not by a blind check. Compare exact-key, loose-key and precondition-checked reuse on wrong-application rate and accuracy.

claim: Published admission and repair rules differ by system and are never compared at equal tokens. The only same-task comparison found (Memp) put error-driven revision of a failed retrieved entry ahead of append-all and success-only filtering (+0.7 reward and 14 fewer steps over the second best). ACE found that small delta edits with helpful/harmful counters avoid the collapse that full rewrites cause. AutoManual stops training a class after 3 successes in a row. Whether execution-verified, outcome-verified or count-threshold admission wins is still open.
agent_test: Run four admission rules (append-all, verified-success, novelty-only, count threshold) plus error-driven repair on one stream at equal tokens.

claim: A store with a minority of bad updates still beats no store, but constant bad updates do not. ACE with a deliberately harmful update on every iteration scored 66.7 vs base 70.7; every 5th iteration 76.1; every 25th 77.8; none 78.3. Accuracy also drifts down as a plan cache fills (92 to 85.5 from 1 to 100 entries in APC). No study measures detection and removal of naturally arising wrong entries with a false-deletion count.
agent_test: Inject known wrong entries at rates of 0, 5, 10 and 25 percent and measure accuracy and how many a utility counter removes, with false deletions.

claim: The gain from a store depends on two gates: whether the base model can write correct entries and use them, and whether the stream repeats structure. Dynamic Cheatsheet: Sonnet and GPT-4o gained, Haiku and GPT-4o-mini gained little or lost; the Game of 24 jump (10 to 99) happened only for the model that found the code routine (Sonnet stayed at 12 to 14). Evo-Memory: gain correlated with within-dataset task similarity (r = 0.717 and 0.563).
agent_test: Estimate recurrence of impasse classes in our stream before building; measure the store gain separately for high- and low-recurrence slices.

claim: The maker of reusable entries has to be strong, while the user can be weak. LATM: GPT-3.5 as tool maker made 0 of 5 valid tools on the hard tasks, mostly tools that worked only on the training cases, while GPT-4-made tools lifted GPT-3.5. Dynamic Cheatsheet: small models could not fill the memory with correct solutions. Buffer of Thoughts lists weak-model initialisation as a limit.
agent_test: If a smaller model must use the store, author and check entries with the stronger model and count that cost.

claim: A store's growth curve is not a smooth power law in the data found. Game of 24 under Dynamic Cheatsheet was a step (10 to 99 once one routine was stored). The new-entry rate of a plan cache over 100 queries fell roughly linearly (75 percent of queries added an entry in the first block, 20 percent in the last), and a straight line fit better than an exponential, which fit better than a power law (derived on 5 points). The human literature says per-participant exponential beats power; Soar's curves were never refit.
agent_test: Track new-entry rate and hit rate per block; fit linear, exponential and delayed-exponential per run and stop adding when the marginal hit-rate gain falls below authoring cost.
